source: AutoX narrative-content workflow — region+province facts grounded in DLT/NSO/DIW/OAE data

regions.narrative: Isan (the Northeast) is Thailand's largest, poorest, and most title-loan-relevant region: 20 provinces sitting in the lowest minimum-wage band (Tier 4, ~฿340-345/day in 2025) with informal-employment shares running 85-92% of all workers — the highest in the country and far above the national norm. Incomes are seasonal and rain-fed, driven by glutinous and hom-mali rice, cassava, sugarcane, and household livestock, so cash flow peaks at harvest and goes thin in the dry months; OAE prices show cassava down ~20-25% YoY against a firmer rice/sugar, a swing that lands directly on borrower repayment capacity. Vehicle fleets are motorcycle-heavy (typically 55-70% of registrations) with relatively few cars and almost no EVs, meaning the realistic collateral book here is pickups and motorcycles owned by farmers, gig riders, and informal traders rather than late-model cars. Two manufacturing/logistics exceptions stand out — Nakhon Ratchasima (Korat), the southern gateway with ~1,800 factories and 112k factory workers, and Khon Kaen, the region's medical, education and logistics hub — while the Mekong-border provinces (Nong Khai, Mukdahan, Nakhon Phanom, Bueng Kan, Ubon Ratchathani) lean on cross-border Laos trade and remittances. For AutoX this is a high-density, thin-ticket market: large informal populations and pickup/moto collateral support volume, but drought, commodity-price swings, and dependence on Bangkok/EEC remittances make Isan's repayment cycle the region most exposed to seasonal and weather shocks.

The North is Thailand's most informal-income, most agriculture-dependent region outside Isan: informal workers run from ~62% of the workforce in Chiang Mai to 91–93% in Nan, Chiang Rai and Mae Hong Son, so most borrowers have no payslip and income arrives by season and by crop price. The economy splits in two — an upper north (Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai, Lamphun, Phrae, Nan, Phayao) built on tourism, services, longan/lychee/garlic/shallot/coffee and the Lamphun electronics estate, and a lower north (Phitsanulok, Nakhon Sawan, Kamphaeng Phet, Phetchabun, Sukhothai, Phichit) that is a rice–sugarcane–cassava–maize bowl. Vehicle dependence is extreme and pickup-heavy: motorcycles are 53–82% of the registered fleet and pickups 17–21%, the classic title-loan collateral, while EV penetration is near-zero outside Chiang Mai — so collateral here is overwhelmingly used ICE motorbikes and farm pickups whose resale value is exposed to fuel and second-hand demand. The dominant credit risks are weather and price: longan and maize prices have swung double digits year-on-year, drought/flood cycles and PM2.5 burning-season haze hit both farm yield and tourism takings at the same time. Tak is a special case — the Mae Sot border SEZ concentrates garment factories and a large migrant-labour and cross-border-trade economy (35,974 factory workers, the region's highest, on a small population). For a title lender the North means seasonal, crop-and-tourism-linked cash flows, thin formal documentation, and pickup/motorbike collateral that is liquid but price-sensitive.

The South is Thailand's rubber, palm-oil and tourism belt, and for a title-lender it is defined by two things: extreme informality and heavy vehicle dependence. Informal workers make up roughly 67-88% of the workforce in every southern province (smallholder rubber tappers, palm and fruit growers, fishers, market traders, tour and resort staff) — incomes that are seasonal, cash, and undocumented, the classic title-loan customer. Household cash flow tracks two volatile prices: rubber (latex/sheet, which recovered ~25-40% YoY in the data) and palm fresh-fruit bunches (which fell ~13-29% YoY), so a single price swing or a monsoon flood can move repayment capacity across whole districts at once. The vehicle base splits the region in two: the Andaman tourism provinces (Phuket, Krabi, Phang Nga) and the deep south (Pattani, Yala, Narathiwat) are overwhelmingly motorcycle economies (63-80% of registrations), while plantation provinces like Chumphon and the rubber heartland run far more pickups (Chumphon 26% pickups) used as working farm collateral. Anchor employers are seafood and rubber/palm processing (Songkhla ~74k factory workers, Surat Thani ~42k, Trang ~24k) plus tourism hubs that swing hard with arrivals. The standing read: collateral quality is good (pickups in plantation zones, well-traded motos elsewhere) but income is price- and season-driven, so PD is correlated to commodity and tourism cycles rather than idiosyncratic — concentration risk to watch, and white-space opportunity wherever rubber/palm cash exists without dense competitor coverage.

The East is Thailand's industrial engine and its fruit basket in one region — a sharp split that title-lending must read carefully. The EEC core (Chonburi, Rayong, Chachoengsao, Prachinburi) holds the country's densest factory belt — Chonburi alone has 3,790 registered factories employing ~220k, Rayong 2,113 (Map Ta Phut petrochemicals + auto/EV) — and pays the top ฿400/day wage tier, with formal employment far above the national norm; here the credit story is wage stability versus the EV transition and US-tariff export exposure that threaten ICE auto-parts and line workers. The eastern fruit-and-border belt (Chanthaburi, Trat, Sa Kaeo) is the mirror image: 79-83% of workers are informal, incomes ride durian/mangosteen/rubber/cassava cycles, and pickups make up a far higher share of the fleet (19-23% vs ~11% in Chonburi) — a strong title-collateral signal, but one whose repayment capacity swings with harvest prices and Chinese fruit demand. Right now rubber is up sharply (+25-40% YoY) while cassava (-20-25%) and palm have fallen, so the same province can carry both rising and falling income pockets. Across all seven provinces motorbikes dominate the registered fleet (54-66%), confirming deep vehicle dependence for daily life and a broad title-loan collateral base. The practical lending map: EEC provinces offer scale and formal wages but cyclical/automation risk in autos; the fruit belt offers high informal vehicle-dependent demand but harvest-price volatility and, in Sa Kaeo/Trat, border-trade sensitivity.

The Central plain and Bangkok metro are Thailand's economic core, but they split into two very different title-lending markets. The inner metro ring — Bangkok, Samut Prakan, Samut Sakhon, Pathum Thani, Nonthaburi — is a dense formal-wage and factory economy (Samut Prakan and Samut Sakhon each register 6,000+ factories; Bangkok alone holds 12.4m registered vehicles, including 272k EVs), where borrowers are salaried, sub-contract, or migrant workers and collateral is plentiful but competition is fierce. The outer central provinces — Ayutthaya, Saraburi, Lopburi, Suphanburi, Kanchanaburi, Ratchaburi, Phetchaburi, Prachuap — flip to a deeply informal, vehicle-dependent profile: informal-worker shares run 72–83%, pickups and motorbikes dominate the fleet, and household income leans on rice, sugarcane, cassava, livestock, fruit and seasonal tourism. This duality matters for risk: metro incomes track the export and manufacturing cycle (US tariffs, automation, flood exposure along the Chao Phraya), while the agricultural belt rides crop prices, drought/flood and harvest timing. Vehicle dependence outside the rail-served metro makes pickups and motorbikes both the lifeline and the natural collateral. The region carries the heaviest AutoX branch footprint in the country, so the opportunity is less white-space and more sharpening segment-level risk pricing.
